summary: Describes how to use the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol as an authentication method in TLS. SRP lets a user prove knowledge of a password without sending it and without needing certificates. This is an informational memo, not a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This lets you prove you know a secret password to a website without ever telling the password itself, like showing you know a secret handshake without saying it out loud.

questions: how to use srp with tls
how does secure remote password work
subtitle: How to log in to a TLS server with a username and password without ever revealing the password.

tldr.problem: TLS authentication relied on certificates, pre-shared keys or Kerberos, which suit poorly the many protocols that already use user names and passwords.
tldr.mechanism: SRP runs inside the normal TLS handshake: the client sends its user name in an extension, the server answers with group parameters, a salt and a public value, and both sides derive a shared premaster secret from the password.
tldr.outcome: A password can be used safely over an unencrypted channel without revealing it to an eavesdropper, and the exchange yields a secret for encryption keys. The RFC is Informational and was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5054 is an Informational RFC that, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted but is updated by RFC 8996. It was written against TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346).

sections.title: Passwords for TLS
sections.content:
When this RFC was written, TLS used public key certificates, pre-shared keys or Kerberos for authentication. These do not suit applications such as IMAP, and since many protocols are built around user names and passwords, safely using them gives an easier route to extra security.

SRP (Secure Remote Password) is an authentication method that allows user names and passwords over unencrypted channels without revealing the password to an eavesdropper. It also provides a shared secret at the end that can generate encryption keys. This document uses the version called SRP-6.
sections.eli5: You can show a guard you know the password without saying it where others can hear, and you both walk away with a secret code for later.

sections.title: The SRP Handshake
sections.content:
SRP uses the standard TLS handshake message sequence. The client sends its user name I in the Client Hello. The server replies with Server Hello, an optional Certificate, and a Server Key Exchange carrying the group parameters N and g, a salt s and its public value B. The client answers with Client Key Exchange carrying its public value A, then both sides finish as in normal TLS.

The server never stores the password. It stores a verifier v, computed as x = SHA1(s | SHA1(I | ":" | P)) and v = g^x % N. User names and passwords are UTF-8 prepared with the SASLprep profile.

Both sides then compute the same premaster secret from the password-derived value. If either side gets it wrong, the Finished messages fail to decrypt and the other party returns a bad_record_mac alert. A client that sees this alert should tell the user the entered user name and password are incorrect.
sections.eli5: The server keeps only a scrambled fingerprint of your password. You each do math with your own secret numbers, and the answers match only if you started from the right password.

sections.title: Extension, Messages and Cipher Suites
sections.content:
SRP adds a TLS extension named srp with value 12. Its data is the user name, opaque srp_I<1..2^8-1>. The key exchange adds a value srp to the KeyExchangeAlgorithm enumeration: the server's ServerSRPParams carry srp_N, srp_g, srp_s and srp_B, and the client's ClientSRPPublic carries srp_A.

Nine cipher suites are defined, in three groups of three. Plain TLS_SRP_SHA_* suites authenticate the server by its possession of the verifier. The SRP_SHA_RSA and SRP_SHA_DSS suites also require a server certificate and a signature over the Server Key Exchange. Implementations MUST implement TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA and SHOULD implement the AES-128 and AES-256 variants of the plain suite.

Four alert uses are described: unknown_psk_identity (115) for a missing extension or an unknown user name, insufficient_security (71) for untrusted group parameters, and illegal_parameter (47) when A % N or B % N is zero.
sections.eli5: The messages are the same envelopes TLS always uses, with a few new slots for the user name and the math numbers.

sections.title: Special Cases in the Hello
sections.content:
A client resuming an SRP session MUST still include the SRP extension, in case the server refuses and needs a full handshake. If the server does resume, it MUST ignore the extension's contents so an attacker cannot swap in a different identity.

If a client offers SRP cipher suites but omits the extension, a server that wants SRP SHOULD return a fatal unknown_psk_identity alert, and the client MAY reconnect with the extension. This lets a client advertise SRP without prompting the user or exposing the user name.

For an unknown user name, the server MAY abort with the same alert, or hide that fact by simulating a verifier: it returns a consistent salt and group for the same name, for example derived with HMAC-SHA1 from a secret seed key, and then rejects the Finished message with bad_record_mac. It should also simulate computation delays.
sections.eli5: If a stranger asks for a secret room that does not exist, a clever guard acts like it exists and says the password was wrong, so nobody learns who has a room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The checks that reject A % N = 0 and B % N = 0 are called CRUCIAL for security and MUST be performed. The private values a and b SHOULD be at least 256-bit random numbers.

The group parameters matter greatly. N MUST be a safe prime and g a generator. An attacker who can compute discrete logarithms modulo N could compromise passwords and TLS sessions, so clients MUST check that N is large enough and SHOULD only accept parameters from a trusted source such as Appendix A. The 1024-bit and 1536-bit groups there MUST be supported.

Other points: anyone who steals a verifier can impersonate the server to that user and attempt a dictionary attack, so servers SHOULD rate-limit guesses; the user name travels in the clear in the Client Hello; and SHA-1 is used here in ways the RFC says collision attacks do not break, with new cipher suites to be defined if that changes.
sections.eli5: Guard the list of scrambled fingerprints, and only play the game with rule books you trust, or a trickster could rig the game.
